introduction-the-source-of-truth-problem.core: If people change the cluster directly (kubectl edit), nobody knows its real intended state. GitOps makes Git the single source of truth: the desired state is declared there, and agents make the cluster match it.

first_principles.problem: A 3 AM `kubectl edit` fixes production, then the next deploy overwrites it, and nobody knows what changed.
truths: Manual changes aren't recorded or reviewed.
Declarative state can be versioned.
Agents can reconcile reality to a declaration.
derivation: An **agent reconciles** the cluster to Git.

analogy.title: A building's official blueprint
analogy.story: Renovations happen by updating the blueprint first; inspectors make the building match it.
analogy.breaks: Emergencies still happen, so you need a fast, sanctioned break-glass path.

example.title: The 3 AM fix, the GitOps way

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: There's always a record, and `git revert` is the rollback.

check.q: What is the 'source of truth' in GitOps?
check.a: The Git repository containing the declarative desired state.

the-evolution-push-based-vs-pull-based-d.core: In push-based CD, the pipeline holds cluster credentials and pushes changes in. In pull-based GitOps, an agent inside the cluster pulls from Git, so credentials never leave the cluster and drift can be corrected continuously.

first_principles.problem: CI systems with admin credentials to every cluster are a huge attack target, and nothing fixes drift after a push.
truths: Credentials outside the cluster widen the attack surface.
A push happens once; reconciliation is continuous.
Agents can see live state.
derivation: **Pull**: agent in cluster watches Git → applies.
CI still builds images and updates **manifests in Git**.

analogy.title: A delivery driver with master keys vs. residents collecting parcels
analogy.story: Pull means each building collects its own parcels from a locker, so no outsider holds every key.
analogy.breaks: The agent still needs Git read access and registry access.

example.title: A new image release
flow: CI commits tag bump to config repo

steps.label: Security
steps.detail: CI never touches the cluster API.

check.q: Why is pull-based deployment considered more secure?
check.a: Cluster credentials stay inside the cluster, so CI doesn't need admin access to it.

gitops-superpowers-self-healing-and-drif.core: Because the agent continuously compares live state with Git, it detects drift (manual changes, deleted resources) and can automatically revert to the declared state. That's self-healing.

first_principles.problem: Manual tweaks accumulate silently until environments differ in ways nobody understands.
truths: Reality diverges from intent over time.
Continuous comparison reveals divergence.
Automatic correction removes snowflakes.
derivation: **Diff** live vs desired on every sync loop.
Use **prune** to delete resources removed from Git.

analogy.title: A thermostat
analogy.story: It constantly measures the temperature and corrects it back to the set point.
analogy.breaks: Self-healing fights legitimate controllers (like HPA changing replicas) unless you ignore those fields.

example.title: Someone scales a deployment by hand

check.a: When the live running state diverges from the declared desired state.

the-agents-argocd-and-flux.core: ArgoCD (a rich UI, Application CRDs, multi-cluster) and Flux (lightweight, composable controllers, Kustomize/Helm-native) are the leading CNCF GitOps agents. Both watch Git and reconcile clusters.

first_principles.problem: You need a tool to implement pull-based reconciliation in practice.
truths: Both are CNCF graduated projects.
They differ in UX and architecture.
Both support Helm, Kustomize and plain YAML.
derivation: **ArgoCD**: Application CRD, web UI, SSO/RBAC, sync waves, ApplicationSets.
Choose by **team UX needs and architecture**.

analogy.title: Two brands of thermostat
analogy.story: One has a big touch screen and app (ArgoCD); the other is small and modular, wired into the house (Flux).
analogy.breaks: Both are good choices. Team familiarity usually matters more than features.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The api namespace tracks apps/api/prod on main.

check.q: Name the two leading CNCF GitOps tools.

controlling-deployment-order-sync-waves.core: Some resources must be applied before others: CRDs before custom resources, migrations before the app. ArgoCD sync waves (annotations) and hooks, or Flux dependsOn, order the apply.

first_principles.problem: Applying everything at once fails: the app starts before its migration, or CRs are applied before their CRDs exist.
truths: Dependencies exist between resources.
Kubernetes applies manifests in no guaranteed order.
Some steps must finish before the next one starts.

analogy.title: Building construction phases
analogy.story: Foundation, then frame, then roof. Each must pass inspection before the next begins.
analogy.breaks: Long chains of waves slow syncs, so only order what truly depends on something.

example.title: Migration before deploy

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The app rolls out only after the migration succeeds.

code.text:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: migrate
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded

example.outcome: dependent resources deploy in the right order.

check.q: How do you run a DB migration before an app in ArgoCD?
check.a: As a Job annotated as a PreSync hook (or in an earlier sync wave).

organizing-your-git-repository-directory.core: Avoid branch-per-environment (it drifts and merges are painful). Prefer directory-per-environment with shared bases and overlays (Kustomize) or values files (Helm), and promote by PR between directories.

first_principles.problem: dev, staging and prod branches drift apart, and promotion merges bring in unrelated changes.
truths: Environments share most config.
Differences should be explicit and small.
Promotion should be a reviewable change.
derivation: **Promote** by updating the image tag in the next overlay.

analogy.title: A master recipe with regional variations
analogy.story: One base recipe, and small cards noting 'less spice for kids' or 'bigger portions for events'.
analogy.breaks: Too many overlay layers become their own maze, so keep the hierarchy shallow.

steps.label: Promote
steps.detail: A PR changes prod's image to v1.5.

code.text:
apps/api/
  base/            deployment.yaml service.yaml kustomization.yaml
  overlays/
    staging/       kustomization.yaml (image: v1.5, replicas: 2)
    prod/          kustomization.yaml (image: v1.4, replicas: 6)

check.q: Why is branch-per-environment discouraged in GitOps?
check.a: Branches drift and promotion merges drag in unrelated changes, making differences hard to see.

the-secret-problem-in-gitops.core: GitOps wants everything in Git, but plaintext secrets in Git are permanent leaks: every clone and every bit of history has them. You need encrypted secrets in Git, or references to an external secret store.

first_principles.problem: Committing a database password, even briefly, exposes it to everyone with repo access, forever, in history.
truths: Git history is permanent and widely replicated.
Base64 isn't encryption.
Secrets must still be declaratively managed.
derivation: Option 2: **reference** an external store (External Secrets Operator + Vault/ASM).

analogy.title: A public noticeboard
analogy.story: You can pin a locked box (encrypted) or a note saying 'key at the front desk' (reference), but never the key itself.
analogy.breaks: If a secret is leaked, rotate it. Deleting it from history isn't enough.

example.title: A Kubernetes Secret committed by mistake
example.outcome: secrets are managed declaratively without exposure.

check.q: Is a base64-encoded Kubernetes Secret safe in Git?
check.a: No. Base64 is encoding, not encryption, and anyone can decode it.

solving-secrets-sealed-secrets-and-sops.core: Sealed Secrets encrypts a Secret with the cluster controller's public key into a SealedSecret that only that controller can decrypt. SOPS encrypts the values in YAML files with KMS, age or PGP, and Flux or Argo decrypt them at apply time.

first_principles.problem: You need secrets versioned in Git alongside everything else, but unreadable to anyone browsing the repo.
truths: Asymmetric encryption lets anyone encrypt and only the key holder decrypt.
Encrypting only the values keeps diffs readable.
Key management is the hard part.
derivation: **Sealed Secrets**: `kubeseal` → SealedSecret CRD → the controller decrypts in-cluster.
**SOPS**: `sops -e` encrypts values with KMS or age; tooling decrypts on apply.

analogy.title: A mailbox with a slot
analogy.story: Anyone can drop a letter through the slot (encrypt with the public key), but only the owner has the key to open the box.
analogy.breaks: Lose the private key and every sealed secret becomes unrecoverable.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only the cluster can decrypt it, while Git holds the encrypted version.

code.text:
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=s3cr3t --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  | kubeseal --format yaml > db-sealed.yaml
git add db-sealed.yaml   # safe to commit

points: Decrypt only in-cluster or with KMS.

check.a: Only the Sealed Secrets controller in the target cluster, which holds the private key.
